ch09.card: Part 8 of 8. Does the thinking really do the work?
ch09.s01.c1: This part is the thinker, a team of note-takers that works in rounds. One round is one lap: look at the whole question, pass notes, think. It is the same team every round.
ch09.s01.c2: We claim the thinking does the work. This chapter tests that claim, on an older design with 12 fixed rounds and a calculator built in.
ch09.s02.c1: Our model scored 73.01 points out of 100 on 6,040 questions kept aside.
ch09.s02.c2: That is 4,410 right. But is it the thinking that earns them? A score alone has nothing to compare with.
ch09.s03.c1: To score it, we use 6,040 questions kept aside. None were used in practice.
ch09.s03.c2: They come in five kinds, from familiar to new. Some have new words.
ch09.s03.c3: They add up to 6,040. The test is called pooled-5. Pooled means mixed into a single score.
ch09.s04.c1: This model was trained with 12 rounds, and at 12 rounds it scores 73.01.
ch09.s04.c2: Now turn the rounds dial down, with no new practice. At 2 rounds, it scores 29.30.
ch09.s04.c3: 1 round: 20.00. The team gets just a single lap.
ch09.s04.c4: 0 rounds, no thinking at all: 0.66. Just 40 right out of 6,040.
ch09.s05.c1: Now turn the dial past its practice, to 24 rounds. That is more laps than it practiced with.
ch09.s05.c2: The score does not rise. It is 72.57, which is 27 fewer right: 4,410 minus 4,383.
ch09.s05.c3: The design we plan to ship adds a learned stop switch, which picks the number of rounds. That switch is built, but never tested.
ch09.s06.c1: A second test, called chain-5: 1,000 multi-step questions kept aside. Multi-step means several sums in a row.
ch09.s06.c2: Each calculator step takes its own round, so cutting rounds should hurt most. In the apple example, a round just for looking is spent before the sums.
ch09.s07.c1: A lesion test: break one part, and see if the answer breaks. If that part really does the work, the answer should fall apart.
ch09.s07.c2: Give the talker, which writes the answer, another question's notes. The score falls to 4.19 on familiar questions.
ch09.s07.c3: Shuffle the notes between questions: 6.80. This is a wiring check. It shows plumbing, not good reasoning.
ch09.s08.c1: Swap add and subtract inside the calculator, which is plain code that does the sums. The answers follow.
ch09.s08.c2: Of 831 answers the swap changes, 830 followed it. The talker copies what the calculator hands back.
ch09.s08.c3: Switch it off: the score is 0.0 on 2,085 questions that need it.
ch09.s09.c1: At zero rounds a model should score near zero. Some runs did not. That is a leak, and a small leak is a warning light.
ch09.s09.c2: An earlier version, copy 200, scored 18.09 with the borrowed Gemma reader, and 1.40 without it. Its other copy, 201, scored 4.49 and 4.34.
ch09.s09.c3: Our copy 400: 0.96 here, 0.66 on all 6,040. The cause is not settled.
ch09.s10.c1: On this one copy, ours scores 5.9 points more than the plain model, our yardstick. That's our subtraction: 73.01 minus 67.12.
ch09.s10.c2: But it took 2.7 times longer to train in this run. That's our division: 6.51 by 2.38 hours. Training hours are the practice time.
ch09.s10.c3: Add a calculator to the plain model, no retraining: 69.62 and 99.0. The gap is 3.39 points, by our subtraction.
ch09.s11.c1: As of Oct 9, one copy at the smallest size is a first result, not proof. One copy is one run from its own random start.
ch09.s11.c2: This is the older design, with 12 fixed rounds and the calculator built in. It says nothing yet about bigger sizes.
